_: Everything a person can choose, and what each choice does. Effects use a fixed vocabulary, handled in main.js: color, material, visible, addon, light, glass, blinds, tv, shade, wall. `check` is where 08_check_configurator.py looks to see that an option changes the room. `code` values go into share links: never reuse or renumber them, only add new ones. A group with `hidden: true` is no longer offered: it keeps its code so old links still read, stays at its default, and themes and rules never set it. Hidden today: the toys, play mat and gaming console (not part of an adult ICU) and the ventilation grilles.

note.text: All finishes shown are easy to clean.
Light that changes through the day like daylight and dims at night. Studies are mixed: a trial of 734 ICU patients found bright light alone didn't reduce delirium.

sources.label: Spies et al., Crit Care Med 2024
Simons et al., Lancet Respir Med 2016

note.text: At night only a soft amber light stays on, so staff can check on the patient with less light in the room.
The bright light over the bed for examinations. It has its own switch: no mode or scene dims it, and Clinical and Emergency modes turn it on. Its brightness is only illustrative.
This is an isolation room. Whatever you choose, the door must be sealed and tested so the room keeps its air pressure.
Glass that switches from clear to frosted, instead of a curtain. Staff can still see in when needed, and there's no fabric to collect germs. Memorial Sloan Kettering's ICU has already done this.

sources.label: Healthcare Design, Memorial Sloan Kettering ICU

note.text: Blinds sealed between the panes of glass replace the curtain.
Or click the switch on the wall next to the door.
Plants stay outside the window, because they aren't allowed near patients with weak immune systems. For greenery inside, add the biophilic wall panel from Place items.
At the patient's eye level from the bed.
The picture is a sample animation.
A concept: the day, date and time in large text, so the patient can keep track of time from bed. It dims at night, shows no patient information, and makes no claim about delirium or sleep.
Animated fish on a screen: the look of an aquarium with no water, fish or cleaning inside the room.

Health guidelines advise against fish tanks near patients, so the screen is the default. If a real tank is wanted, this one is sealed in the wall and cleaned from outside the room. Infection control should decide.
Not recommended for isolation rooms, because an outside door breaks the room's air seal. Best for standard rooms.

A sliding door that opens about 1.6 m, so the patient can be taken outside in their bed or a wheelchair. Concept only: no structural or fall-safety design has been done, and a confused patient would need someone with them.
A floor-to-ceiling built-in wardrobe with no top for dust to collect. The entrance stays clear. Its size and clearances are a concept, still to be reviewed.
Uses the existing bathroom next to W1. The fixtures are suggestions that need expert review.
Shows our concept for ceiling air vents, not SSMC's design. Display only: no air moves.

A concept: a sensor that would hear a groan or a call for help through the closed door and send the nurse a notice, so they look through the glass before putting on protective gear to go in. Patients on a breathing machine or sedated may not make sounds, and alarms can set it off. Sounds would be classified on the device and never stored. Simulated here, with no microphone.

Wipe-clean acoustic panels: two on the family zone's back wall and three ceiling tiles over it, clear of the vents, the lights and the bed. They absorb some of the sound that bounces round the room. In Acoustic comfort mode their effect is made up, not measured. A real one needs infection-control and manufacturer sign-off before it goes in an ICU. Five UK ICUs measured were all louder than WHO's hospital guideline, which the authors judged out of reach in an ICU; that is an observational study, and no fitting was tested.

The glazed front in laminated acoustic glass, sealed all round, so staff still see in while less corridor talk comes through. It stays clear glass: the smart glass and curtain still work. Its effect in Acoustic comfort mode is made up. A real one needs infection-control and manufacturer sign-off before it goes in an ICU.

Dampers that slow the door and the wardrobe's doors over their last few centimetres, so they don't bang. The door still closes and seals by itself. Its effect in Acoustic comfort mode is made up. A real one needs infection-control and manufacturer sign-off before it goes in an ICU.

Rubber isolators behind non-critical kit, here the TV, so a hum doesn't carry into the wall. Never on the monitor, pumps, ventilator or any medical device. Its effect in Acoustic comfort mode is made up. A real one needs infection-control and manufacturer sign-off before it goes in an ICU.

A clip on each line's route round the patient, with a tag in its line's colour: on the side rails' tops for the IV line, the feeding tube and the ECG leads, a holder at the head end for the respiratory circuit, and a guide on the bed frame for urinary drainage, never on a moving rail. They keep each route where staff expect it, so a line is quicker to trace. They don't secure a line, and they change no line, connector or device. Expected, not shown.

A shallow tray in the ceiling over the bed: square tiles inside a border, a line of light round its edge and a row of small downlights by the window. The line of light takes the colour of the room's light. Its border keeps clear of the ceiling lights, the pendant and the wardrobe. With the printed sky on, the sky fits inside it. A real one needs the ceiling's services, structure and infection-control requirements checked.

One flush white panel on the wall behind the bed head, with two wide screens for staff and a line of light beneath. Its screens show a still, marked simulated: there's no reading on them. The patient monitor stays on the pendant, working, and the panel never stands in for it. It's for staff, because a patient lying in the bed can't see the wall behind their head.

A flush white panel round the TV on the wall the patient faces, with a strip of screen over the TV and a line of light beneath. The TV sits on the panel, and everything on it keeps working. The strip shows a still, marked simulated: no real names, plans or times.

A desk for the care team, against the wall by the window, out of the keep-clear areas and the route to the bed: a rounded white top on a timber-and-white cabinet, a screen and keyboard, a second screen on an arm, and a lit rail. Its screens show a still, marked simulated, with no patient's name or diagnosis. In W1 the visitor chair moves nearer the window to make room for it. A real one needs its place, power, data and infection-control requirements checked.
A cabinet for the patient's own things, with a white top and a timber front, at the bed head on the window side: clear of the pendant and its outlets, and of the space round the bed.

For staff: the staff panel shows made-up heart rate, oxygen saturation, blood pressure, breathing rate and temperature, with care tasks and equipment. The bedside monitor keeps running beside it, and no alarm changes. The patient keeps the day, the date and the time.

For the patient: the day, the date and the time on the TV, the care team by role and a simple plan for the day over it, and two buttons that open the communication board and family connection. A sedated patient gets no buttons. The staff panel rests on a dark standby screen.
A scene across the patient wall, in place of everything that isn't needed now: the one chosen under Transform my environment, or the desert from the sample comfort passport.

One switch for the staff panel and the patient wall in the Future ICU fittings: who the wall is for right now. Room modes move it too: Clinical turns it to Clinical, Comfort to Relaxation, and Emergency turns the patient wall off, and every scene with it. Simulated: every value is made up, and no screen stands in for the bedside monitor.

One choice sets the patient wall, the ceiling above the bed and the room's light together, and changes slowly, over a few seconds. Off goes back to how the room was. Each scene is drawn in code. Without the patient wall, the scene shows on the TV. A room mode, Quiet now and the patient's state come first, and Emergency turns every scene off.

Three flush discs on the ceiling: over the bed, inside the door and over the middle of the room. Open room intelligence to see what each would cover, and to try two made-up events. A concept: they sense nothing here, and nothing watches or listens.

Flush channels on the ceiling and on the wall behind the bed head: one for power and data, and a separate one for medical gas, which never shares a channel with anything electrical. A docking spot is marked on the floor where the ventilator stands, fed from the pendant. Illustrative routes, not an engineering design.

profile._: Suggest a room: answers pick a theme, then rules adjust it. Rules use `sets`, the group-to-option map themes use, because `effects` only change the scene and never reach the share code, comparison or undo. A rule with no `when` always applies. `when` is one set of conditions, or a list where any one will do. A higher tier locks what it sets against lower tiers. `because` is shown to the person, so it talks about the room and never about the patient. Every answer has to be used by a `when` or listed in `noEffect`: 08_check_configurator.py fails otherwise. This never changes the room and doesn't recommend care.

themes.because: Family Suite is the starting look when family stay close.
Desert Sanctuary is the starting look for a longer stay.
Calm Clinical is the plain starting look.

rules.because: A patio stays your own choice. Its notes cover the pressure, structure and fall-safety questions.
The larger sofa-bed is left out, so less stands on the floor. The route through the room hasn't been measured.
A sofa-bed gives visitors somewhere to stay.
Softer, warmer light and nothing moving on a screen, for a quieter room.
A low night light keeps the room easy to read after dark.
A warmer wardrobe finish for a longer stay.

cleanAir._: The wall comfort control's card: filters and UV-C in the air handling plant. A concept, with nothing drawn in the room. The rows are a copy of ventilation.clean_air in spec/icu_spec.json; 12_check_pacs_state.mjs fails if they differ. Each row's basis is in REPORT.md, under Clean air, which the card links to.

titles.isolation: Clean air for this isolation room · concept
titles.patient: Clean air for this ICU room · concept

sources.label: The report: the basis for each row

rows.label: Supply filters
rows.isolation: Two stages in the air handling unit: MERV 8 or better, then MERV 14 or better after the cooling coil.
rows.patient: Two stages in the air handling unit: MERV 8 or better, then MERV 14 or better after the cooling coil.

rows.label: Air leaving the room
rows.isolation: All exhausted through a HEPA filter, then straight outdoors on its own fans. None is recirculated.
rows.patient: Return air goes back to the air handling unit and through both filter stages again.
rows.basis: Isolation: HFG Part E 2026 (Class N); DHA Part D Table 5. ICU room: assumed from where the filters sit

rows.label: UV-C on the cooling coil
rows.isolation: Lamps just after the coil, to stop mould growing on it. The access door has a safety switch.
rows.patient: Lamps just after the coil, to stop mould growing on it. The access door has a safety switch.
rows.basis: HFG Part E 2026: encouraged for cooling coil surfaces

rows.label: UV-C in the exhaust duct
rows.isolation: An extra step with the HEPA filter. It replaces neither the filter nor the air changes.
rows.patient: None. Upper-room UV-C is the guidance's option for critical care rooms, and isn't modelled.
rows.basis: DHA Part D (Class N exhaust); HFG Part E 2026: an additional measure, not mandatory; CDC 2003: supplemental only

rows.label: Not proposed
rows.isolation: Fogging, ozone, ionisers and photocatalytic cleaners. Nothing is sprayed or released into the room's air.
rows.patient: Fogging, ozone, ionisers and photocatalytic cleaners. Nothing is sprayed or released into the room's air.
rows.basis: CDC 2003: no disinfectant fogging in patient-care areas. HFG Part E 2026 doesn't encourage electronic or photocatalytic cleaners, because of ozone

rows.label: Not designed
rows.isolation: The HEPA grade, lamp output, safe filter changes, and where the plant and ducts go.
rows.patient: The HEPA grade, lamp output, safe filter changes, and where the plant and ducts go.
